retrospective: Session built the eval-pack plugin from scratch across 13 tasks — plugin manifest, three shell scripts, three skills, HTML/CSS/JS templates, GitHub Action, README, and e2e tests. What went well: TDD with e2e test caught format issues immediately; code review subagents caught the critical XSS vector in renderMarkdown before it shipped; the round accumulation model for regeneration was clean and held up under testing. What was slow: the transcript format mismatch (real Claude Code uses nested .message.* but scripts assumed flat .content/.model/.usage) wasn't discovered until generating this very eval pack — the e2e test used a flat fixture that passed. That's a spec gap: the test fixture format diverged from the real format. The grep -c double-output bug and jq range/index bug were caught during code review and required careful rewrites. The XSS fix required three separate patches (escapeHtml, renderMarkdown, screenshot onclick) — fragmented because they were caught across different review passes.
friction: Repo was empty at session start — no existing conventions to follow, which is both fast and risky. The absence of integration tests against real Claude Code transcripts was the biggest gap: the e2e test used a hand-crafted fixture in the flat format, masking the .message.* nesting that real transcripts use. This wasn't catchable from the spec. Future friction: the scripts still count input tokens without cache tokens (cache_read_input_tokens, cache_creation_input_tokens are ignored), so totalTokens underreports heavily for long sessions. The GitHub Action two-path orphan branch logic is correct but fragile — any concurrent PR could race on the gh-pages branch checkout. No CI configured in this repo, so the test suite only runs on demand.
promptQuality: Initial prompt was directional but underspecified on two dimensions that caused rework: (1) the transcript format — no mention of the real .message.* nesting structure, so scripts were written to a simpler assumed format; (2) the XSS threat model — no mention that analysis.json content comes from Claude itself (trusted) vs. user-controlled repos (untrusted), which affected how aggressive escaping needed to be. What would have helped front-loaded: the actual Claude Code transcript JSONL schema (a 5-line example), and a note that pagesBaseUrl and gh CLI are optional so setup should degrade gracefully. The phased plan (13 tasks, spec → plan → subagent-driven execution) was the right structure — it forced interface decisions before implementation and made the review subagents effective.
